extracted.subtask_description: USPTO examiner guidance for evaluating subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, with emphasis on the 'improvement' consideration for computer-implemented inventions, including machine learning/AI claims and the Step 2A (Prong One/Prong Two) analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification disclosure sufficiency for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the specification provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or a technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art. Conversely, if the specification explicitly sets forth an improvement but only in a conclusory manner (i.e., a bare assertion of an improvement without the detail necessary to be apparent to a person of ordinary skill in the art), the examiner should not determine that the claim improves technology or a technical field. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and Ex Parte Desjardins examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding the specification discloses an improvement in technology, evaluate whether the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement by including the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim itself does not need to explicitly recite the improvement (e.g., a claim need not say 'thereby increasing the bandwidth of the channel'), but it must include limitations that embody the improvement. Use the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to determine whether the claim reflects the improvement. See Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Symantec Corp. and Ex Parte Desjardins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the claim 'as a whole' (ordered combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the claim 'as a whole' — in other words, evaluate the claim as an ordered combination without ignoring the requirements of the individual steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to avoid oversimplifying claims by treating them at too high a level of generality and thereby dismissing potentially meaningful technical limitations. Consider each step/element and how they combine to provide the improvement. Cite: McRO and Ex Parte Desjardins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss additional elements as generic computer components without analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether a claim improves technology, do not dismiss additional elements as mere 'generic computer components' without considering whether such elements confer a technological improvement to a technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly for improvements to computer components or computer systems, analyze whether claimed elements meaningfully contribute to the technological improvement rather than being treated as generic. Ex Parte Desjardins emphasizes this caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish particular solution vs. mere idea/outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the extent to which the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration overlaps with the 'particular machine' and 'mere instructions to apply an exception' analyses. Claims that recite a particular way to achieve a result (a concrete solution) are more likely to be viewed as improving technology. See DDR Holdings and related discussion in MPEP § 2106.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One / Prong Two framework application
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Step 2A two-prong analysis: Prong One — determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea, mathematical concept); Prong Two — determine whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application (i.e., whether the claim reflects an improvement so that the exception is not present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Prong One finds a judicial exception but Prong Two finds the claim (as a whole) integrates that exception into a practical application (e.g., by reflecting a technological improvement disclosed in the specification), then the claim is outside the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO). Ex Parte Desjardins is an example where Prong One found an abstract idea and Prong Two found the claim integrated the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification examples of machine-learning improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize machine-learning-specific improvements disclosed in the specification as potential technological improvements: e.g., training a model to learn new tasks while protecting knowledge of previous tasks (addressing 'catastrophic forgetting'), reduced storage usage, reduced system complexity, and preservation of performance attributes across tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Appeals Review Panel in Ex Parte Desjardins credited benefits including reduced storage, reduced system complexity and streamlining, and preservation of performance attributes during subsequent computational tasks as technological improvements disclosed in the specification. Such improvements can show the claim reflects an improvement in how the ML model operates and are not necessarily subsumed in an identified mathematical calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements via parameter adjustments to ML models
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize disclosures that improvements to computer component or system performance are achieved based on adjustments to parameters of a machine learning model associated with tasks or workstreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2106.05(a) (examples xiii and xiv) identifies as examples: (xiii) improved ways of training a machine learning model protecting prior-task knowledge while effectively learning new tasks; and (xiv) improvements to computer component or system performance based upon adjustments to parameters of a machine learning model. Use these as concrete indicia of technological improvement where disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precedential case examples as instructive benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Federal Circuit and PTAB precedents as examples of claims that have been found to improve technology (and thus not be directed to an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: Enfish (self-referential table data structure), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial expression animation), Visual Memory (enhanced computer memory system), Finjan (virus scanning), SRI Int’l v. Cisco (detecting suspicious activity via network monitors), DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Thales Visionix, and Ex Parte Desjardins. Compare claimed invention to these precedents for analogous improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider BRI (broadest reasonable interpretation) when assessing reflection of improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation to determine if the claim reflects an improvement in technology or a technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BRI to assess whether the claim scope encompasses the improvement disclosed in the specification; ensure analysis does not improperly narrow or unduly broaden the claim when relating claim elements to the disclosed improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement consideration overlaps with other §101 considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the 'improvement' inquiry overlaps with other §101 considerations (e.g., particular machine, 'mere instruction to apply' the exception), and use those evaluations to assist determining whether a claim satisfies the improvement consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a claim reflects a technological improvement, also evaluate whether the claim involves a particular machine (see MPEP § 2106.05(b)) or whether it is merely instructing to apply an exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)). These related analyses can provide supporting reasoned conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite a technological solution to a technological problem are 'more than apply it'
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify claims that recite a technological solution to a technological problem as examples of claims that amount to more than merely applying an abstract idea or law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Thales Visionix, and Ex Parte Desjardins illustrate when the combination of limitations provided a technology-based solution that overrode routine or conventional behavior or eliminated complications in prior solutions. Look for claim language that specifies how interactions or configurations are manipulated to yield an improved, concrete technical result.
